MetaCheck Report

The Forecasting Proficiency Test: A General Use Assessment of Forecasting Ability

2026-11-21 · Metacheck 0.4.4.28

2to fix5to check0to decide by hand1fine7not applicable

To fix (2)

To fix Ethics Approval Check

What we found

1 of 1 paper appeared to involve live data collection and lacked an ethics approval statement.

Show details

Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, but it was not present:

In each CQ and TQ wave, participants were assigned one of the five parallel blocks in the QEF.

Prior to Wave 1, we preregistered several exclusion criteria designed to filter out inattentive participants (see study preregistration).

During Wave 1, the first time participants completed multiple forecasting questions in a single sitting, median response times for the QEF questions ranged from 2.09 to 5.47 (IQR of medians = [2.76, 3.91]).

In each study, we recruited people to participate in a Rapid Fire Forecasting Challenge.

Participants were recruited between May 3, 2023 and May 15, 2023.

We recruited N = 100 participants via advertising on social media.

Participants had mean age of 40.67, SD = 14.07, 3,798 (61.5%) female, 2,170 (35.1%) male, 158 gender variant / non-conforming (2.6%), 8 something else (0.1%), 44 (0.8%) prefer not to say.

Participants were recruited between September 1, 2023 and September 15, 2023.

We recruited N = 1,199 participants via social media.

In the U-shaped condition, participants were paid $12.50 for completing the first wave, $5 for completing the second, and $12.50 for completing the third.

In the escalating condition, participants were paid $5 for completing the first wave, $10 for completing the second, and $15 for completing the third.

And in the backloaded condition, participants were paid $5 for completing each of the first two waves, and $20 for completing the third.

Participants who began with Wave 0 were recruited between September 1 st and 7 th of 2023, and completed two forecasting questions in each of the QEF and PEF.

Participants not in the Wave 0 condition were recruited between Procedure.

Participants are asked to assess the probability that several events occur within a series of increasing time horizons.

In this task, subjects are given a series of general knowledge problems with two possible answers.

To fix Codebook Check

What we found

  • We parsed 419 variable definitions from codebook/README files.
  • 539 of 1602 data columns (34%) are documented in a codebook; 1063 are not.
  • 4 matched columns have a conflicting or ambiguous label that needs resolution.
Show details

This module checks whether each extracted data column is documented in a codebook or README, and flags documented variables that never appear in the data.

We examined 11 codebook/README/label sources and 1602 data columns across 52 files.

Ins_list_1 yes For this survey, we will ask you to make predictions about a series of different events. The 10 participants who make the most accurate predictions on average during this survey will each win a $25 bonus prize. If more than 10 participants are tied for most accurate, we will select at random such that 10 of the most accurate participants will each receive a prize. When making predictions, we won’t simply ask you to make one prediction, but a series of predictions by filling in the blank in questions like this: there is a 25% chance the result will be ___ or ${e://Field/g_l}. Let’s look at an example. In this example, we want you to predict the average temperature (Fahrenheit) in New York City in November 2024. To make a prediction about this question, we might show you a sentence like: There is a 25% chance the average temperature in New York City will be ___ degrees (Fahrenheit) or ${e://Field/g_l} in November 2024. If you answer 50, that means you are saying that you believe there is a 25% chance that the average temperature in New York City will be 50 degrees (Fahrenheit) or ${e://Field/g_l} in November 2024. Put another way, you would be saying that there is a 75% chance the average temperature in New York City will be ${e://Field/g_l_alt} than 50 degrees (Fahrenheit) in November 2024. For each question, we will provide you with a link. This link will tell you both how the outcome of the question will be determined, and can also help you research your answer by learning about recent and historical trends for this problem. For example, we might tell you that we will determine the actual average temperature in New York City in November 2023 by using the weather.gov monthly average temperature table for Central Park (New York City). This link also provides historical temperature averages for every month going back to 1869. Now it’s your turn to try: What will be the average temperature (Fahrenheit) in New York City in November 2024? For each percentage listed below, your answer should indicate you believe there is that percent chance the outcome will be ___ or ${e://Field/g_l}. Ins_list CFQ Forecasting.qsf labelled

Ins_list_1 yes For this survey, we will ask you to make predictions about a series of different events. The 10 participants who make the most accurate predictions on average during this survey will each win a $25 bonus prize. If more than 10 participants are tied for most accurate, we will select at random such that 10 of the most accurate participants will each receive a prize. When making predictions, we won’t simply ask you to make one prediction, but a series of predictions by filling in the blank in questions like this: there is a 25% chance the result will be ___ or ${e://Field/g_l}. Let’s look at an example. In this example, we want you to predict the average temperature (Fahrenheit) in New York City in November 2024. To make a prediction about this question, we might show you a sentence like: There is a 25% chance the average temperature in New York City will be ___ degrees (Fahrenheit) or ${e://Field/g_l} in November 2024. If you answer 50, that means you are saying that you believe there is a 25% chance that the average temperature in New York City will be 50 degrees (Fahrenheit) or ${e://Field/g_l} in November 2024. Put another way, you would be saying that there is a 75% chance the average temperature in New York City will be ${e://Field/g_l_alt} than 50 degrees (Fahrenheit) in November 2024. For each question, we will provide you with a link. This link will tell you both how the outcome of the question will be determined, and can also help you research your answer by learning about recent and historical trends for this problem. For example, we might tell you that we will determine the actual average temperature in New York City in November 2023 by using the weather.gov monthly average temperature table for Central Park (New York City). This link also provides historical temperature averages for every month going back to 1869. Now it’s your turn to try: What will be the average temperature (Fahrenheit) in New York City in November 2024? For each percentage listed below, your answer should indicate you believe there is that percent chance the outcome will be ___ or ${e://Field/g_l}. Ins_list CFQ Forecasting.qsf labelled

To make a prediction about this question, we might show you a sentence like: There is a 25% chance the average temperature in New York City will be ___ degrees (Fahrenheit) or ${e://Field/g_l} in November 2024. If you answer 50, that means you are saying that you believe there is a 25% chance that the average temperature in New York City will be 50 degrees (Fahrenheit) or ${e://Field/g_l} in November 2024. Put another way, you would be saying that there is a 75% chance the average temperature in New York City will be ${e://Field/g_l_alt} than 50 degrees (Fahrenheit) in November 2024. For each question, we will provide you with a link. This link will tell you both how the outcome of the question will be determined, and can also help you research your answer by learning about recent and historical trends for this problem. For example, we might tell you that we will determine the actual average temperature in New York City in November 2023 by using the weather.gov monthly average temperature table for Central Park (New York City). This link also provides historical temperature averages for every month going back to 1869. Now it’s your turn to try: What will be the average temperature (Fahrenheit) in New York City in November 2024? For each percentage listed below, your answer should indicate you believe there is that percent chance the outcome will be ___ or ${e://Field/g_l}. Ins_list CFQ Forecasting.qsf labelled

ins_q1 What will be the average temperature (Fahrenheit) in New York City in April 2024 ? In this example, we want you to predict the average temperature (Fahrenheit) in New York City in April 2024. If you answer 50, that means you believe there is a 25% chance that the average temperature in New York City will be less than or equal to 50 degrees (Fahrenheit) in April 2024. Put another way, you would be saying that there is a 75% chance that the average temperature in New York City will be greater than 50 degrees (Fahrenheit) in April 2024. For each question, we will provide you with a link. This link will tell you both how the outcome of the question will be determined, and can also help you research your answer by learning about recent and historical trends for this question. For example, we might tell you that we will determine the actual average temperature in New York City in April 2024 using the weather.gov monthly average temperature table for Central Park (New York City). This link also provides historical temperature averages for every month going back to 1869. Now it’s your turn to try: What will be the average temperature (Fahrenheit) in New York City in April 2024 ? For each percentage listed below, your answer should indicate you believe there is that percent chance the outcome will be ___ or less. CFQ Forecasting.qsf
ins_q2 Based on your answer, you believe: A. There is a 5% chance the average temperature in New York City will be less than or equal to ${q://QID177/ChoiceTextEntryValue/1} degrees (Fahrenheit) in April 2024, which means you believe there is a 95% chance the average temperature in New York City will be greater than ${q://QID177/ChoiceTextEntryValue/1} degrees (Fahrenheit) in April 2024. B. ins_q0 In this section, we will ask you several forecasting questions in the continuous form at . As you have seen previously, we will ask you to make a series of predictions about questions like this: What will be the average temperature (Fahrenheit) in New York City in April 2024 ? You will then see a series of percentage values, and for each one, your answer should indicate you believe there is that percent chance the outcome will be ___ or less. For example, if you put the number 50 for 25%, that would indicate you believe: There is a 25% chance the average temperature in New York City will be 50 degrees (Fahrenheit) or less in April 2024 . Would you like to review a further explanation of this format and practice with this example before you start answering questions? CFQ Forecasting.qsf
ins_p0a In this section, we will ask you several forecasting questions in the probability format . As you have seen previously, we will ask you to predict the probability of one or more events occurring in the future. For example, we might ask the following: What is the probability that the average temperature in New York City in March 2024 will be above 44 degrees (Fahrenheit)? CFQ Forecasting.qsf
ins_p0b Or we might ask the same question as follows: What will the average temperature (Fahrenheit) in New York City in March 2024 be? CFQ Forecasting.qsf
ins_p0c Would you like to review a further explanation of this format and practice with this example before you start answering questions? CFQ Forecasting.qsf

ins_c6 If the average temperature in New York City in March 2024 turns out to be above 44 degrees , that might suggest the average temperature in April 2024 will be higher than if the alternative case were true : that the temperature in March 2024 is less than or equal to 44 degrees . So you might make a prediction of a higher temperature in April 2024 for the first question than the second question. This section will have two sets of questions broken up into three parts: a continuous part, a probability part, and a conditional part. The continuous and probability parts will both count towards your overall accuracy. For the conditional parts, we will only score your accuracy for the question on which the conditional aspect is true. So in this example, if the average temperature in New York City March 2024 is above 44 degrees , only the first question above would count towards your overall accuracy. PFQ Forecasting.qsf

ins_q0 Let’s briefly review the continuous form at. As you have seen previously, in the continuous form at , we will ask you to make a series of predictions about questions like this: What will be the average temperature (Fahrenheit) in New York City in April 2024 ? You will then see a series of percentage values, and for each one, your answer should indicate you believe there is that percent chance the outcome will be ___ or less. For example, if you put the number 50 for 25%, that would indicate you believe: There is a 25% chance the average temperature in New York City will be 50 degrees (Fahrenheit) or less in April 2024 . The order of your predictions should correspond to the order of the percentages. The prediction you make for 95% should be equal to or greater than the prediction you make for 50%, and the prediction you make for 50% should be equal to or greater than the prediction you make for 5%. Note: Please don’t use any non-numeric characters, including commas, dollar signs, or percentage symbols, in entering your responses. Would you like to review a further explanation of this format and practice with this example before you start answering questions? PFQ Forecasting.qsf
ins_p0a Let's briefly review the probability format . As you have seen previously, in the probability format , we will ask you to predict the probability of one or more events occurring in the future. For example, we might ask the following: What is the probability that the average temperature in New York City in March 2024 will be above 44 degrees (Fahrenheit)? PFQ Forecasting.qsf
ins_p0b Or we might ask the a similar question as follows: What will the average temperature (Fahrenheit) in New York City in March 2024 be? PFQ Forecasting.qsf
ins_q3 In this section for continuous questions , we will also ask you to provide a prediction as your best single estimate for a question. Your answer to questions like this should be the one you think is most likely to be as close as possible to the eventual outcome. What will be the average temperature (Fahrenheit) in New York City in April 2024? What is your best single estimate for this question? PFQ Forecasting.qsf
ins_q4 Based on your answer, your best single estimate for the average temperature in New York City in April 2024 is ${q://QID324/ChoiceTextEntryValue} degrees (Fahrenheit) . Is that correct? If not, you may press the back button below to return to the previous screen. If yes, proceed to the next page. PFQ Forecasting.qsf
ins_c1 In this section, in addition to continuous and probability format questions, we will ask you conditional questions . These combine both continuous and probability forecasts by asking you to make a continuous prediction conditional on a probability outcome. Here is an example. First, as part of the continuous questions , we will ask you to provide a prediction as your best single estimate for a question. Your answer to questions like this should be the one you think is most likely to be as close as possible to the eventual outcome. What will be the average temperature (Fahrenheit) in New York City in April 2024 ? What is your best single estimate for this question? PFQ Forecasting.qsf

ins_cond_46_0_1 Let’s briefly review the conditional format . In this section, in addition to continuous and probability format questions, we will ask you conditional questions . These combine both continuous and probability forecasts by asking you to make a continuous prediction conditional on a probability outcome. Here is an example. First, as part of the continuous question , we will ask you to provide a prediction as your best single estimate for a question. Your answer to questions like this should be the one you think is most likely to be as close as possible to the eventual outcome. For example, we might ask: What will be the average temperature (Fahrenheit) in New York City in April 2024 ? What is your best single estimate for this question? Second, you will be asked to make a probability forecast . For example, we might ask: What is the probability that the average temperature in New York City in March 2024 will be above 44 degrees (Fahrenheit)? Finally, we will ask you the continuous question again twice, each time conditional on the two possible outcomes from the probability forecast . For example, we might ask: What is your best estimate for the average temperature in New York City in April 2024, if the average temperature in New York City in March 2024 is above 44 degrees (Fahrenheit)? and What is your best estimate for the average temperature in New York City in April 2024, if the average temperature in New York City in March 2024 is less than or equal to 44 degrees (Fahrenheit)? Would you like to review a further explanation of this format and practice with this example before you start answering questions? PFQ Forecasting.qsf

Q347 We will also ask you to provide your best estimate for the average temperature in New York City in April 2024, if the average temperature in New York City in March 2024 is less than or equal to 44 degrees (Fahrenheit) . PFQ Forecasting.qsf
Q348 If the average temperature in New York City in March 2024 turns out to be above 44 degrees , that might suggest the average temperature in April 2024 will be higher than if the alternative case were true : that the temperature in March 2024 is less than or equal to 44 degrees . So you might make a prediction of a higher temperature in April 2024 for the first question than the second question. This section will have two sets of questions broken up into three parts: a continuous part, a probability part, and a conditional part. The continuous and probability parts will both count towards your overall accuracy. For the conditional parts, we will only score your accuracy for the question on which the conditional aspect is true. So in this example, if the average temperature in New York City March 2024 is above 44 degrees , only the first question above would count towards your overall accuracy. PFQ Forecasting.qsf

This question would only count towards your overall accuracy if the average temperature in March in New York City is, in fact, above 44 degrees. Based on your answer, if the average temperature in March is less than or equal to 44 degrees (Fahrenheit) , your best prediction for the average temperature in New York City in April 2024 is ${q://QID347/ChoiceTextEntryValue} degrees . This question would only count towards your overall accuracy if the average temperature in March in New York City is, in fact, less than or equal to 44 degrees. Is that correct? If not, you may press the back button below to return to the previous screen. If yes, proceed to the next page. PFQ Forecasting.qsf

Intro Welcome to our study! We are researchers interested in differences in people’s skill at making forecasts about future events. As such, the study will consist of various forecasting problems and cognitive tasks. This is a brief introductory survey that will familiarize you with the types of tasks we will ask you to do. By completing this survey, you will become eligible to participate in the full study, which includes seven (7) additional surveys that will be distributed each week over the next two months. For each of those weekly surveys, you will be paid a baseline amount, beginning with $5 for the first survey and going up to $20 for the final survey. In total, if you complete all seven, you will be paid $70 . Additionally, each survey will include performance bonuses based on the accuracy of your forecasts as well as your scores on the cognitive tasks. The top 25 performers in the weekly surveys will each receive a $25 bonus . Though there is no base payment for this introductory survey, there is a potential to win a performance bonus! This survey has eight items that will count towards your final score. The top 50 performers across all eight items will each receive a $10 bonus . When an item will count towards your score, this will be indicated at the top of each page, along with how many items remain. In total, it is possible to earn an additional $185 bonus on top of the $70 baseline amount for completing the entire study! Please press the button below to continue. Wave 0.qsf

Put another way, you would be saying that there is a 75% chance that the average temperature in New York City will be greater than 50 degrees (Fahrenheit) in April 2024. IC University of Pennsylvania RESEARCH PARTICIPANT Informed Consent Form Protocol Title: Forecasting Proficiency Test Principal Investigator: Philip Tetlock 3720 Walnut Street (215) 746-8541 Emergency Contact: Kaitlyn Coffee kcoffee@sas.upenn.edu Sponsor Open Philanthropy Research Study Summary for Potential Participants You are being invited to participate in a research study. The research study is being conducted to test different ways of assessing people’s probabilistic reasoning ability and forecasting skills. This test will consist of answering forecasting questions in a variety of topical areas as well as completing cognitive tasks that are related to decision-making, logical thinking, understanding graphs and figures, identifying patterns, and estimating probabilities. This study will be divided into seven parts. Each takes approximately one hour to complete. If you successfully complete each section, we will invite you back to resume the study one week later. If you agree to join the study, you will be asked to complete the following research procedures: You will be shown a series of forecasting questions and asked to make predictions for each question. You will also be asked to complete various tasks in the form of deciding between two options, multiple choices, filling out the blank, and estimating a value by indicating it on a slider or a graph. You will get paid based on the number of parts completed. If you complete the entire study, you will be paid $70. You will also have the chance to win several bonuses of $10 and $25. The total potential bonus compensation will be up to $185, depending on your performance. The benefit of this study is that you will get to experience making probability forecasts and various cognitive challenges. After the study is complete, we will provide you with some information about how well you performed on each task relative to other participants in the study. There are no known risks associated with participation. Your participation is voluntary, and you should only participate if you completely understand what the study requires and what the risks of participation are. You should ask the study team any questions you have related to participating before agreeing to join the study. If you have any questions about your rights as a human research participant at any time before, during or after participation, please contact the Institutional Review Board (IRB) at (215) 898-2614 for assistance. Please note that there are other factors to consider before agreeing to participate such as additional procedures, use of your personal information, costs, and other possible risks not discussed here. You are free to decline or stop participation at any time during or after the initial consenting process. Why am I being asked to volunteer? You are being asked to take part in a research study because we wish to understand the impact of forecasting questions on the general public. Your participation is voluntary which means you can choose whether or not to participate. If you do not understand what you are reading, do not provide your electronic consent. Please contact us and we can explain anything you do not understand, including any language contained in this form. If you decide to participate, you will click next after reading this page. By doing so, you will be considered to have signed the consent form. Please keep a copy of this form for your records. You may ask to have this form read to you. What is the purpose of the study? The purpose of the study is to learn more about forecasting by creating a bank of forecasting questions and tasks using forecasting-related skills that can be used in many other studies. How long will I be in the study? There are seven parts of the study that each need to be completed approximately one week apart. Each part takes approximately 1 hour to complete. If you are unable to complete a section within a single session, you may be able to return later and finish it, however each section will have an end date. If you do not complete the task prior to the end date, you may not be invited back to complete later sections. What am I being asked to do? You will use a platform to make probability forecasts on the likelihood of future events. E.g. What the price of Gold in U.S. dollars will be on a given date. You will also complete various tasks related to decision-making, logical thinking, reading graphs, identifying patterns, and estimating probabilities. For example, you may need to decide between two options, selecting a best answer from several choices, indicating your estimation of probabilities on a slider, or fill out numeric values based on the information given. What are possible risks or discomforts? There are no known risks or discomforts associated with participating in this study. What if new information becomes available about the study? During the course of this study, we may find more information that could be important to you. This includes information that, once learned, might cause you to change your mind about being in the study. We will notify you as soon as possible if such information becomes available. How will I benefit from the study? By participating in this study, you will get to experience making probability forecasts and various cognitive challenges. Will I be paid for being in this study? You will begin with a brief introductory survey. After that, we will begin inviting you back at weekly intervals to complete seven additional sessions. If you complete all seven sessions, you will be paid a total of $70. You will also have an opportunity to win performance bonuses during each session, totaling up to $185. If you stop your participation, you will get paid for all sections of the study you had completed prior, but may not be invited back for future sections, in which case you will not be paid for the remaining study sections. Please note that the University of Pennsylvania is required to report to the IRS any cumulative payments for participation in research studies that exceed a total of $600 in a calendar year. Will I have to pay for anything? No. When is the Study over? Can I leave the Study before it ends? You are encouraged to complete all seven parts of the test in seven weeks. You may choose to stop whenever you wish. Please note that you will only get paid for the parts that you complete. This study may also be stopped at any time because: The Primary Investigator feels it is necessary for the welfare, rights, or safety of participants. Such an action would not require your consent, but you will be informed if such a decision is made and the reason for this decision. The Sponsor or the study Principal Investigator has decided to stop the study. If you decide to participate, you are free to leave the study at any time. Could I be withdrawn from the study? You could be removed from the study if you fail attention checks. How will my personal information be protected during the study? We will do our best to make sure that the personal information obtained during the course of this research study will be kept private. However, we cannot guarantee total privacy. Your personal information may be given out if required by law. If information from this study is published or presented at scientific meetings, your name and other personal information will not be used. The Institutional Review Board (IRB) at the University of Pennsylvania will have access to your records. Confidentiality will be secured on a platform and will be de-identified to maintain the identity of the participant. What may happen, in the future, to my information collected on this study? Your information will be de-identified prior to storage for future use. De-identified means that all identifiers have been removed. The information could be stored and shared for future research in this de-identified fashion. It would not be possible for future researchers to identify you as we would not share any identifiable information about you with future researchers. This can be done without again seeking your consent in the future, as permitted by law. The future use of your information only applies to the information collected on this study. If you change your mind, we will not be able to destroy or withdraw your information that was shared because all identifiers would have already been removed. Who can I call with questions, complaints or if I’m concerned about my rights as a research participant? If you have questions, concerns or complaints regarding your participation in this research study or if you have any questions about your rights as a research participant, you should speak with the Principal Investigator listed on page one of this form. If a member of the research team cannot be reached or you want to talk to someone other than those working on the study, you may contact the IRB at the number on page one of this form. When click the button below to move to the next page, you are agreeing to take part in this research study. This means that you have read the consent form, your questions have been answered, and you have decided to volunteer. Your signature also means that you are permitting the University of Pennsylvania to use your personal information collected about you for research purposes within our institution. You are also allowing the University of Pennsylvania to disclose that personal information to outside organizations or people involved with the operations of this study. Please save or print a copy of this form for your records. Wave 0.qsf

To check (5)

To check Non-Significant P Value Check

What we found

We found 6 non-significant p values that should be checked for appropriate interpretation.

Show details

Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is ‘no effect’, ‘no difference’, or that groups are ‘the same’ after p > 0.05.

It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is ‘not significantly’ different, although this just restates that p > 0.05.

Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values.

Text Sentence
p = .25 Appendix K has figures which show their median forecasts, 50% prediction intervals (interval between p = .25 and p = .75 quantiles), and 90% prediction intervals (interval between p = .05 and p = .95 quantiles) for each wave and block of CQ questions with vertical lines representing the question resolution and annotations showin their sample standardized S-score.
p = .75 Appendix K has figures which show their median forecasts, 50% prediction intervals (interval between p = .25 and p = .75 quantiles), and 90% prediction intervals (interval between p = .05 and p = .95 quantiles) for each wave and block of CQ questions with vertical lines representing the question resolution and annotations showin their sample standardized S-score.
p = .95 Appendix K has figures which show their median forecasts, 50% prediction intervals (interval between p = .25 and p = .75 quantiles), and 90% prediction intervals (interval between p = .05 and p = .95 quantiles) for each wave and block of CQ questions with vertical lines representing the question resolution and annotations showin their sample standardized S-score.

For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see:

Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742.

Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167.

For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see Improving Your Statistical Inferences.

README Files

README files are a way to document the contents and structure of a folder, helping users locate the information they need. You can use a README to document changes to a repository, and explain how files are named. Please consider adding a README to each repository or including ‘README’ in the name of your overview document.

Unclassified Files

1 file is of a kind metacheck does not know, so it is not counted as data, code or documentation: CODEOWNERS. This is no problem in itself.

Study/Repository Mismatch

The studies named in the manuscript do not match how the repository’s files are grouped: the manuscript names studies (ex1a, ex1b, pilot1b) with no matching files in the repository; the repository separates out studies (ex1, pilot2, pilot1, ex8) not named in the manuscript. Check that every study has its own clearly-named folder or file prefix, and that the folder names match how the manuscript refers to each study.

File Naming

File names should be machine-parseable: no spaces or special characters, and every file should be classifiable by name or extension. We found 39 naming problems that should be fixed, and 60 files with a naming suggestion (not required, but a good habit).

Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid setwd() in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. No setwd() calls were found in any of the code files.

Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid install.packages() in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an renv.lock/DESCRIPTION for R, a requirements.txt for Python). install.packages() calls were found in 4 code files.

Parsable code

All R-type code files (.R, .Rmd, .qmd) could be read in. There were no parsing issues.

To check Data Check

What we found

  • We classified 5077 files: 3198 data, 95 code, 46 documentation, 1737 materials, 1 unknown.
  • We found 2693 tabular data files and extracted 1602 columns from 52 of them.
  • We grouped the files into 7 study groups (ex1, ex2, ex3, ex8, pilot1, pilot1a, pilot2), plus 4 collection-level files (README/ro-crate metadata).
  • 2638 tabular data files could not be read because they were not downloaded. This can happen for private repositories or failed downloads; you can also pass local_path to point at a local copy.
  • Repository https://github.com/forecastingresearch/fpt exceeds the 500 MB per-repository budget: downloaded the smallest files up to the cap, 2643 files omitted. Raise max_download_size to include more.
  • 1 R workspace file (.RData/.rda) contains no reusable tabular data — only fitted models or saved session objects. Such files need R (and the exact packages used) to open and are not machine-readable. Share the underlying data as CSV (or a documented .sav/.dta) with a codebook so it can be reused without R: Forecasting Proficiency Test R Environment.RData.
  • 2 files read as a table but are not a usable rectangular dataset (data_cognitive_tasks/cache/session_info.RData: the file has no data rows or columns; data_pilot_cognitive_tasks/cache/session_info.RData: the file has no data rows or columns). No columns were extracted and they were not sent to the LLM. Share the underlying data as a plain rectangular table (one header row, one column per variable) with a codebook: data_cognitive_tasks/cache/session_info.RData, data_pilot_cognitive_tasks/cache/session_info.RData.
  • 505 trial-level data files (E-Prime / Inquisit / jsPsych / Behaverse) were recognised. These are per-participant records of a behavioural task, so they are not listed as separate datasets. Nothing is deleted. We ran automated data-quality checks on 1602 columns; 26 columns have at least one potential issue (17 columns with numeric values stored as text; 8 columns with no observed values (entirely empty); 6 columns whose name suggests personal information; 1 column with inconsistent category casing). 2 files are a Qualtrics survey export (696 rows look like previews/unfinished responses to review). 2 of 2 spreadsheet files have at least one formatting issue (colour coding, merged cells, empty rows/columns, or an offset header).
Show details

This module classifies repository files and, for tabular data files available locally, extracts each column’s type and summary statistics.

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.

We examined 1602 columns across 52 data files.

Issues Identified

28 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

About the personal-information flags. These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

  • Column names are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (email, telefoonnummer, geboortedatum, …). A column called phone_number flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
  • Values are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
  • Free text is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means look at this column. Where the data is already de-identified (an ip column reading Anonymized, a name column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

Spreadsheet formatting such as colour, merged cells, and blank rows/columns is not preserved when data are read programmatically or exported to CSV. Store data as a plain rectangular table (one header row, one column per variable, no colour-encoded meaning) so it is machine-readable.

Careless Responding

No file could be screened for careless responding.

What this does not cover. Only 0 of 52 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

All details of the Reproducibility Check

This module assesses whether the paper’s code could be run on its data, and — because execute = TRUE — actually ran it. We examined 7 R code files.

Run order

A dependency cycle was detected among 5 files (Enhancing reliability in the identification of forecaster talent.R, Forecasting Proficiency Test Code.R, Psychometric properties of probability and quantile forecasts.R, data_cognitive_tasks/fpt.Rmd, data_pilot_cognitive_tasks/fpt.Rmd): each reads a file another writes, so no run order satisfies all of them. This must be resolved before the code can run.

Order File Runs after Basis
1 FPT Forecasting Pilot.Rmd — none
2 FPT Forecasting.Rmd — none

File paths

34 data paths in the code do not work in the repository as deposited. We pointed them to where the file is, so the code could run: scores_quantile.csv to data_forecasting/processed_data/scores_quantile.csv (in Enhancing reliability in the identification of forecaster talent.R); scores_probability with pre-set bins.csv to data_forecasting/processed_data/scores_probability with pre-set bins.csv (in Enhancing reliability in the identification of forecaster talent.R); scores_quantile.csv to ../data_forecasting/processed_data/scores_quantile.csv (in Forecasting Proficiency Test Code.R); scores_probability with pre-set bins.csv to ../data_forecasting/processed_data/scores_probability with pre-set bins.csv (in Forecasting Proficiency Test Code.R); scores_quantile.csv to ../data_forecasting/processed_data/scores_quantile.csv (in Psychometric properties of probability and quantile forecasts.R); scores_probability with pre-set bins.csv to ../data_forecasting/processed_data/scores_probability with pre-set bins.csv (in Psychometric properties of probability and quantile forecasts.R); session.csv to metadata_tables/session.csv (in data_cognitive_tasks/fpt.Rmd); session_restarts.csv to metadata_tables/session_restarts.csv (in data_cognitive_tasks/fpt.Rmd); data_checkpoints.csv to metadata_tables/data_checkpoints.csv (in data_cognitive_tasks/fpt.Rmd); subject_id_group.csv to metadata_tables/subject_id_group.csv (in data_cognitive_tasks/fpt.Rmd), and 24 more. The code should be changed, because as written it does not find these files. The code reads files that are only inside Additiona Versions of Figure 8.zip, and no script unpacks it. We unpacked it in its folder before the run. So that others can run the code as deposited, start the code with a line that unpacks it (such as unzip("Additiona Versions of Figure 8.zip") in R), or upload the files unpacked. 1 reference matched several files sharing a name and could not be resolved by study group or folder; it was left unrewritten and flagged.

Files the deposit does not hold

The scripts that did not run through read 1 data file that is not in the deposit, and no script of the deposit writes: itnames.csv.

Execution

The code was run. Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 7 scripts: 0 ran without error, 0 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions. 7 scripts were not started, or stopped early, because the time for all scripts together had run out. The checks before this one had left 0 sec before the time limit, too little to copy the repository, install its packages and run its scripts (at least 15 min), so none of that was done.

More detail

Power Analysis Check

No power analyses were detected.

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen’s d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.
