3.4. Forecasting Proficiency and Construct Validity

Three of our cognitive tests are among the most ubiquitous and generalizable measures of general intelligence: MR, Shipley-A, and Shipley-V (g-measures). We can use them to benchmark whether any other measures better predict forecasting performance than these standard g-measures. We did this by comparing a first model that uses only the g-measures as predictors (p n ) in eq. 8 to a second model that adds additional predictors. We calculated the proportion of variance in ScA nk attributable to the additional predictors above and beyond the g-measures as: where g refers to the g-measure only model and g+ refers to the additional predictors. 12The model with only g-measures produced R² µ 0,n0 = .41.

The g+ model that added just M SA n from TQs more than doubled the explained variance in CQ accuracy, ∆R² µ 0,n0,g = .42, indicating there is a large amount of variability in forecasters' CQ accuracy that is predictable by TQ accuracy, but not g-measures. Figure 3 shows ∆R² µ 0,n0,g for each other cognitive test score as a single predictor added to the g-measures. Tests such as DN, BU and ADMC-DR each accounted for 5-8% more variance in CQ accuracy above and beyond g-measures, more than twice as much as cognitive tests used in ACE and HFC like BN and NS. The only cognitive test used in ACE and HFC to perform similarly was CRT, which is consistent with a recent study that found CRT is more than just numerical reasoning (Meyer et al. 2024). These results provide evidence that our newly developed cognitive tests explain more about what drives forecasting proficiency than these g-measures or the numerical reasoning tasks common in prior forecasting tournaments. 0.00 0.02 0.04 0.06 0.08 0.10

3.5. Proposing Test Versions

Results have indicated that a) the QEF produces accuracy scores with superior reliability to the PEF, b) historical standardization facilitates combining questions on different scales into a composite score without requiring a large sample to standardize individual question scores, and c) TQ accuracy is the best predictor of CQ accuracy, but cognitive tests can provide complementary predictive information. Based on these results, we propose five different versions of the FPT which vary in how heavily they rely on TQs versus cognitive tests. For consistency, we chose to make each version approximately one hour in length, a somewhat arbitrary choice designed to balance collecting sufficient information with a manageable test length. To maintain this approximate length across test versions, we examined the response times of the forecasting questions and cognitive tests. During Wave 1, the first time participants completed multiple forecasting questions in a single sitting, median response times for the QEF questions ranged from 2.09 to 5.47 (IQR of medians = [2.76, 3.91]). Detailed response time results for QEF questions can be found in Appendix J.

Cognitive test response times can be found in Table C1. We used this information to create five test versions which are outlined in Table 5. R² µ 0,n0 values for the cognitive tests alone are also included, which provides an estimate of the immediate informativeness of each version before TQ forecasting questions resolve. We prioritized cognitive tests that performed well in the dominance analysis results, had relatively short durations, and had a viable AIG versionfoot_7 or did not have high levels of possible exposure in the population. 14 However, the dominance analysis results suggest that, beyond DN, the specific choice of cognitive tests is not particularly important.

3.5.1. Cross-Validation

To ensure test scores based on these FPT versions effectively predict forecasting question accuracy for new participants and forecasting questions, separate from the data on which the models were trained, we performed a five-fold cross-validation. The folds were each defined based on the order conditions in Table 1. Four of the order conditions were used as a training sample to estimate the model in eq. 8, with one testing order condition held out for validation. For example, when order condition 1 was held out, the model was trained on data from order conditions 2-5, and predictions were made on data from order condition 1. This partitioning is natural because it means that in each fold, the model is trained and tested on a separate set of forecasters and forecasting questions-neither the forecasters or CQs the models are trained on appear in their testing samples.

Because we wished to keep proposed FPT versions to approximately one hour in length, none of them could include all of the TQs, so we bootstrapped the procedure. For each order condition and proposed FPT version, we randomly selected a subset of TQs for each participant equal to the number of proposed TQs associated with that FPT version and repeated the procedure 500 times.

In each iteration, we used the trained model to predict accuracy scores on the testing sample:

Figure 4 shows the distributions of R² µ 0,n0 across the 500 bootstrapped iterations for each of the five proposed FPT versions both by order condition (which defined the folds) and across all order conditions. Two reassuring results emerge: (1) the results are highly consistent across order conditions, and (2) the distributions across the 500 bootstrap iterations are relatively narrow. These results indicate strong criterion validity that was consistent across all five folds.

FPT versions 1-3 performed best with mean R² µ 0,n0 between .74 and .77 across all order conditions, while there were diminishing returns in versions 4 and 5 (mean R² µ 0,n0 < .70). 3.7. Individual Forecaster Performance

For demonstration purposes, we randomly selected one bootstrap iteration for FPT Version 3 and compared the QEF forecasts from the CQ waves of the forecasters with the best, median, and worst ˆ ScA n . Appendix K has figures which show their median forecasts, 50% prediction intervals (interval between p = .25 and p = .75 quantiles), and 90% prediction intervals (interval between p = .05 and p = .95 quantiles) for each wave and block of CQ questions with vertical lines representing the question resolution and annotations showin their sample standardized S-score. This allows us to visualize the forecasts of forecasters at the top, middle, and bottom of FPT score distributions.

The best forecasters consistently produced median forecasts close to the question resolution values. They also appear to be well calibrated, in that they produced sensible prediction intervals which bracketed the resolutions of the questions about as often they are supposed to (e.g., the resolution was within their 50% prediction interval in three out of six cases for Figure K1). The weaker forecasters did not as consistently center their forecasts on the question resolutions and were more likely to produce incoherent forecasts. For example, in Figure K1, the worst forecaster's median prediction for the FAO meat question was outside of their prediction intervals, indicating that their quantiles were non-monotonic. See Zhu et al. (2026) for more discussion of this phenomenon.

3.9. Categorical Predictions

A final outstanding question is how well test components discriminate forecasters in different ranges of the skill distribution. We used three thresholds of M SA n from the CQ waves to define the ranges of interest: the 10th, 50th, and 90th percentiles. We used two approaches to test how well predictor variables discriminated whether forecasters were above or below each threshold: a standardized mean differences (Cohen's d) approach and a signal detection theory approach.

3.9.1. Standardized Mean Differences

We calculated Cohen's d for test components comparing groups of forecasters who were above and below each specified threshold. This method is useful for determining which specific predictors might be especially informative about high or low proficiency forecasters. Figure 7 shows absolute Cohen's d values comparing forecasters above and below the specified M SA n thresholds from the CQ waves for the predictors used in the dominance analysis in Table 4. Most predictors were better at discriminating forecasters below the 10th percentile than above the 90th percentile. This was especially true for TQ mean accuracy (M SA n ).

However, the effect sizes for discriminating forecasters above the 90th percentile were quite large as well, with only three d values below 0.5 and several approaching 1.0.0.5 1.0 1.5 2.0 T Q A c c u r a c y A D M C -D R D N -C B U H a r d M R G L C F S C R T N S L F B N Predictor Absolute Cohen's d Range 90th Percentile 50th Percentile 10th Percentile Note: Error bars represent 95% confidence intervals.

3.9.2. Signal Detection Theory

For the signal detection analysis, we fit binary logistic regression models that predicted whether forecasters were above or below each threshold and produced ROC curves. An ROC curve shows the sensitivity, or the proportion of correct positive classifications out of total positive cases, and specificity, or the proportion of correct negative classifications out of total negative cases. Sensitivity and specificity trade off depending on whether one is willing to tolerate more false positives or false negatives. For example, if we are trying to predict the probability that a forecaster is above the 90th percentile of M SA n from the CQ waves, and we want to be very careful to limit the number of forecasters below the 90th percentile that we incorrectly include, we could insist on clearing a high bar for specificity. The corresponding sensitivity would then tell us how many forecasters above the 90th percentile we correctly included and how many we missed by setting such a conservative threshold. If, on the other hand, we wanted to limit the number of forecasters above the 90th percentile that we miss out on, even if it means incorrectly including some forecasters below the 90th percentile, we could insist on a high sensitivity. The corresponding specificity would tell us how many forecasters below the 90th percentile we incorrectly included. The area under the curve (AUC) is a global measure of how well a classification model performs across all levels of sensitivity and specificity. Perfect classifications would yield an AUC of 1.0, while random guessing would have an expected AUC of 0.5.

Logistic regressions used predictors from FPT Version 3 using the same cross-validation logic as prior analyses. For each fold, 16 we fit three logistic regression models in the training samples: one for each of the specified thresholds. Each model was then used to predict the probability participants in the testing sample were above or below the specified thresholds. 17 ROC curves were based on sensitivity and specificity for testing sample predictions.

Figure 8 shows ROC curves for predictions in the testing samples. Consistent with the Cohen's d results, these models were best able to discriminate forecasters below the 10th percentile, with AUCs in the range of .90 to .95. However, they were also able to accurately discriminate forecasters above the 90th percentile, albeit not quite as well, with AUCs ranging from .73 to .81. 4. Discussion

How much can we learn about the proficiency of a forecaster in just one hour? As it turns out, quite a lot. The FPT is capable of explaining approximately 75% of the variance in individual forecasters' performance across a variety of real-world forecasting questions from different domains. Prior to the FPT, the gold standard for identifying talented forecasters was to hold months-long forecasting tournaments among hundreds of forecasters. The FPT can not only be administered to a single forecaster in just one hour, but also can explain even more about their forecasting proficiency than running them through a typical forecasting tournament would.

4.1. Test Components

The FPT is not just informative, but also customizable. It can contain combinations of both reusable real-world forecasting questions and standalone cognitive tests. The versions of the FPT with the strongest criterion validity, as measured by its ability to predict individual differences in accuracy on out-of-sample forecasting questions, relied primarily on these questions. However, scores based on different blocks of questions were only moderately exchangeable. Transforming raw FPT scores to percentiles based distributions normed on different question blocks led to errors, on average, of approximately eight percentile points in how individuals compared to the rest of the test development sample. Combining slightly fewer real-world forecasting questions with a handful of more stable cognitive tests reduced these errors to approximately five percentile points with minimal loss in criterion validity. Cognitive tests also address the cold start problem: the cognitive tests can be scored immediately, providing a preliminary, albeit weaker measure of forecasting proficiency right away without having to wait for forecasting questions to resolve.

4.1.1. Superiority of QEF One of the key results from this project, explored in greater depth by Zhu et al. (2026), is how much more reliable accuracy scores from the QEF are than the scores from the PEF. However, unlike scoring rules for the PEF, such as the Brier and logarithmic scoring rules, S-scores, the proper scores used to evaluate QEFs, are sensitive to the scale of the variable being forecasted. This makes them challenging to combine into a composite person-level score. We solve this challenge with a method we refer to as historical standardization. Historical standardization standardizes both the forecasts and question resolutions prior to scoring for accuracy based on each question's historical time series. The resultant S-scores are scale-free, and can thus be combined into composite person-level composites.

It is important to note that the benefits we find in the QEF are psychometric: QEFs are better for measuring forecasting proficiency, but that does not imply they produce more accurate forecasts.

More research is needed to compare how the accuracy of forecasts might vary as a function of elicitation format. The conclusions presented in this paper are focused on person-level forecasting proficiency measurement.

4.1.2. Item Exposure and Automatic Item Generation

The FPT is intended to be a publicly available resource, but this poses a potential problem: item exposure. If testees become too familiar with the specific questions on some of the cognitive tests, that would invalidate those tests as measurement instruments. Fortunately, our results demonstrate that two of the most informative cognitive tests, denominator neglect and Bayesian updating, are conducive to Automatic Item Generation, which means their content can change dynamically each time they are administered.

This was a significant factor in prioritizing their inclusion in the FPT.

4.2. Identifying Elite Talent

The FPT can reliably identify the best forecasters in the population. However, it is even more successful at identifying the worst forecasters, which suggests there may be room for improvement in elite talent identification. All of the results in this paper rely on parametric linear modeling frameworks. Given the high degree of total variance we are able to explain in forecasters' accuracy, it is unlikely more complex nonlinear or nonparametric models would provide substantial gains across the full population distribution, but there is potential to increase the signal-to-noise ratio specifically in the upper range of the distribution. Follow-up research may wish to consider the extent to which predictive performance can be improved for elite forecasting talent.

4.3. Limitations and Future Directions

The FPT was an ambitious and expensive project. To optimize cost effectiveness, we chose to limit data collection to instruments that could serve as potential test components as much as possible.

Because of this, our results speak most directly to forecasting proficiency for the types of forecasting problems that can be administered on a test: continuous time series questions with time horizons on the order of weeks to months, rather than years. Future research should seek to generalize the usefulness of the FPT to other types of forecasting problems and longer time horizons.

4.3.1. Construct Validity

The purpose of the FPT project was primarily empirical, which is why we prioritized criterion validity over construct validity. However, our results do provide some insight about the notion of forecasting proficiency as a psychological construct, and point towards important new research directions worth pursuing. Several newly developed cognitive tests, such as denominator neglect and Bayesian updating, as well as previously validated tests, such as the cognitive reflection test (Frederick 2005) and the adherence to decision rules subscale of the Adult Decision-Making Competence Inventory (Bruine de Bruin et al. 2007), predicted forecasting proficiency better than common measures of general intelligence and numerical reasoning ability.

This is evidence that these tests tap into skills that distinctly drive forecasting proficiency, and provides a direction for future research more focused on theoretical construct validity.

Additionally, our results say little about the dimensionality structure of forecasting proficiency.

Like the big forecasting tournaments, we intentionally operationalized forecasting proficiency by using a diverse set of questions that come from a variety of domains. The purpose of this choice was to maximally separate forecasting skill from domain expertise. However, forecasting proficiency may well be inseparable from domain expertise. Future research should focus on clearly operationalizing forecasting domains of interest, rather than remaining agnostic to their idiosyncrasies.

4.4. The Future of Forecasting in Psychology

Human forecasting ability is a topic that has generated substantial interest in recent years (Tetlock and Gardner 2015, Atanasov and Himmelstein 2023). However, most recent advances in the field came from studies that were not truly designed to study the psychology of forecasting, but rather the role of crowd wisdom in broader forecasting systems (Benjamin et al. 2023 , Mellers et al. 2015b).

Beyond creating a new gold standard instrument for measuring forecasting proficiency, the FPT project also shows what is possible with dedicated psychological research on human forecasting. We hope that our results not only help humanity make better forecasts, but inspire more psychologists to continue to study how better forecasts can be made.

1. The questions must be timeless, where timelessness is defined as being reusable for an arbitrary resolution date. For example, "What will the price of gold be on December 1, 2022" is a timeless question, because the date can be changed to any other future date and remain a sensible question. A non-timeless question would be "Who will the United States Supreme Court rule in favor of in the case of Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard?" because once this question resolves, it cannot equivalently be asked again for a different future time horizon.

2. The questions must be resolvable, where resolvability refers to the existence of one or more databases that can be used to determine the outcomes of questions, and that can be reported to participants so they clearly understand how the outcome of the question will be determined.

3. We also checked how regularly resolvability databases were updated. Any database that was updated inconsistently or irregularly was omitted.

4. Questions that could be asked about multiple different geographic locations were prioritized. For example, "What will the pm2.5 air quality rating be for Beijing, China on August 1, 2023 be?" Can be asked equivalently about regions other than Beijing.

5. Questions that featured highly duplicative content were de-duplicated.

This procedure ultimately left us with a set of 140 questions under consideration for Pilot Study 1A and 1B. A list of these questions can be found at https://osf.io/q2e94/. We next wanted to filter these 140 questions down 36 questions to be used in the primary study. We wanted a set of questions that was diverse content wise, and did not clearly favor any particular domain expertise. To accomplish this, we sought to collect a sufficiently large amount of pairwise observations between all possible pairs of questions and analyze correlational patterns between the questions. In each study, we recruited people to participate in a Rapid Fire Forecasting Challenge. People were randomly given a sequence of forecasting problems and could answer as many or as few as they wished. Because we didn't want people to invest substantial time, forecasting problems were timed. If participants did not respond before the timer expired, they were moved to the next question. They were not given any baseline compensation for participation, but for each question they answered, they were entered into a lottery for which they could win a monetary prize. They were also awarded additional entries for making accurate forecasts.

A.1.1. Pilot Study 1A.

Pilot Study 1A was a testing and planning study for Pilot Study 1B. Besides testing the study program and recruitment approach, we also wanted to get a ballpark estimate of how feasible it would be to collect a large number of pairwise observations for all pairs of the 140 questions.

Participants. Participants were recruited between May 3, 2023 and May 15, 2023. We recruited N = 100 participants via advertising on social media. We did not collect demographic information during the pilot.

Procedure. We randomly selected 50 of the 140 questions we planned to use in Pilot Study 1B. Participants who registered were randomly assigned a sequence of questions. For each question, they had three minutes to provide a single best estimate for the outcome (all questions were about continuous numerical outcomes), as well as provide a rating using a continuous slider that ranged from 1 to 100 in terms of their familiarity with the question; their confidence in their prediction; how much the forecast depended on the particular time of week, month, or year (seasonality); and how much the difficulty in making a prediction about that question is a result of their lack of personal knowledge rather than lack of predictability ("aleatoryness"). If they did not submit a response within three minutes, they were moved to the next question. All questions had resolution dates at the end of May 2023. For an example of an question, see Figure A1.

For each question, any participant who submitted a response to that question was entered into a lottery.

Each lottery drew five winners who each won $20 each. There were separate lotteries for each question.

The forecasters above the 80 th percentile in accuracy forecasts for each question also received an additional four lottery entries for that question. The forecasters in the 60 th to 80 th percentile received three additional entries, the forecasters in the 40 th through 60 th percentile received two additional entries, and the forecasters in the 20 th through 40 th percentile received one additional entry. The Forecasts were scored using mean absolute error, MAE. Where f represents a forecast and o the outcome:

Results. In addition to testing the procedure, the primary statistical goal of Pilot Study 1A was to estimate how many total participants we would need to recruit to get a large number of pairwise observations for each pair of questions. To accomplish this, we focused on the number of questions participants answered in the pilot study, M = 8.54, SD = 12.58. We modeled these counts by fitting a negative binomial model on the count of how many problems participants to estimate parameters for an expectation (µ = 8.54) and dispersion (θ = 0.47).

We used these parameter estimates to conduct a simulation study. In each iteration of the simulation we began by simulating participants one at a time. Each simulated participant was represented by a random draw from the negative binomial distribution defined by the parameters estimated from Pilot 1A: µ = 8.54, θ = 0.47. This produced a count outcome, which represents the number of questions that simulated participant responded to. Based on that count, we randomly sampled integers between 1 and 140, representing the question indices that participant would randomly have seen as a participant in the study, and we recorded the question indices that participant responded to, and, more specifically, saved all pairs of questions that participant answered. The simulation then proceeded to generate another simulated participant and repeat the procedure. Within each iteration, we repeated this process until the mean number of pairwise observations between pairs of question indices was greater than 100, at which point the iteration terminated and a new iteration began. The simulation was conducted over 50 iterations.

Results indicated that to achieve a mean of 100 observations for all possible pairs of 140 question indices, the mean number of total participants required would be 8,481, SD = 281.8. The smallest number of pairwise observations across the 50 iterations had a mean of 66.32, SD = 2.75. The primary conclusion of this simulation is that if we wished to achieve, on average, 100 pairwise observations between all pairs of 140 questions, we would need to recruit approximately 8,500 participants.

A.1.2. Pilot Study 1B. Pilot Study 1B repeated the same core design of Pilot Study 1A, but it used all 140 questions instead of just 50, and the goal was to examine the correlational patterns of responses between questions to determine if any potentially loaded onto particular domain knowledge that would favor groups with particular specialized expertise over others if used in the primary study. Despite collecting additional data, analyses for Pilot Study 1B focused primarily on the accuracy of the forecasts (scored by MAE ), and as a secondary check on the subjective familiarity ratings. The other variables were collected for potential exploratory analyses and not used in planning subsequent studies, and no analyses involving these variables are reported here.

Participants.

Based on the results of Pilot Study 1A, we were targeting recruitment of 8,500 participants, but with a primary goal of getting as many pairwise observations between each pair of questions as possible.

Recruitment ran from June 26, 2023 through July 18, 2023, recruiting N = 6,295. We wound up with a mean of 99.72 observations for each pair of questions, SD = 7.13, with a minimum of 73. So, although we undershot our target sample size, we functionally achieved our goal of getting an average of 100 observations per pair of questions. Participants had mean age of 40.67, SD = 14.07, 3,798 (61.5%) female, 2,170 (35.1%) male, 158 gender variant / non-conforming (2.6%), 8 something else (0.1%), 44 (0.8%) prefer not to say.

Procedure. The procedure was identical to Pilot Study 1A, except with 140 questions instead of 50.

Results. MAE scores were standardized within question (sMAE ) and winsorized at values of 5 or greater, implying that the forecast was 5 standard deviations less accurate than the mean accuracy for that question, to reduce the influence of outliers on subsequent analyses. Mean sMAE scores were 0.53, SD = 2.27. Mean familiarity ratings were 27.11, SD = 27.45. The correlation between accuracy and familiarity ratings was r = -0.07, suggesting familiarity had a weak correlation with accuracy (lower sMAE scores).

To determine the extent to which specific questions might potentially differentiate specialized expertise, and therefore should be excluded, we conducted exploratory factor analyses (EFAs) on the sMAE scores and familiarity ratings. We began by conducting a parallel analysis for each set of scores to determine the appropriate number of factors. In each case, results suggested that three factors were represented at a level greater than chance (see Figure A2 and Figure A3 for scree plots from these analyses).

In each case, questions with the largest factor loadings had very clear interpretations for one of the first two factors: these questions were highly specialized financial and economic forecasting problems. We refer to this factor as the economic factor.

The economic factor was the first (largest) factor for the sMAE scores, with 53 questions having factor loadings over 0.40, suggesting accuracy on these questions was highly mutually correlated. Questions with exceptionally large factor loadings included the closing yield for U.S. Treasuries, the closing value of the Turkish Lira against the U.S. Dollar and the closing stock price of Mercado Libre.

The other two factors didn't have such distinct interpretations, nor as many questions with such high factor loadings for sMAE. The second factor, which we refer to as a general interest factor, had 18 questions with loadings over 0.40. Questions with large factor loadings for the second factor included an question about how many migrants will arrive in Europe via the Mediterranean Sea, autonomous vehicle collisions in California, and the number of ACLED recorded protests in Lebanon. The questions with the largest loadings on the third factor, which we refer to as simply other (10 questions with loadings of at least 0.40) were about OPEC's crude oil production, the number of new privately owned housing units in the U.S., and the U.S.

Bureau of Labor Statistics nonfarm employment rate.

The pattern was similar for the familiarity ratings, except in this case the economic factor was the second factor rather than the first. In this case, we refer to the first factor as the general interest factor, and 92 questions had factor loadings of 0.40 or larger. The questions with the largest loadings were about protests in China, and Influenza cases in Qatar. The second factor, which was the economic factor, had 49 questions with loadings over 0.40 (32 of which also had loadings over 0.40 for sMAE ). Questions with the highest loadings included the closing value of the S&P 500, the widest closing spread on 10-year Treasurys below the yield on 2-year Treasurys, and the closing price of Mercado Libre (also one of the largest factor loadings for accuracy). Only three questions had factor loadings over 0.40 for the third factor (other), which were how many travelers with the TSA screen, what will the presidential approval rating be, and what will the U.S.

combined box office gross be.

Table A1 is a correlation matrix between the factor loadings for sMAE and familiarity. Worth noting in particular is that the correlations for the same factors (economic and general interest) across the two score types (sMAE and familiarity) are quite large and positive, particularly for the economic factors, and also large and negative between factors both within and between score types.

Discussion. The key takeaway from the results of Pilot 1B is that, among the 140 questions we initially filtered, a large proportion appear to uniquely filter a specialized type of expertise around finance and economics. Because the goal is not to develop a financial literacy test, but a generalized test of forecasting proficiency, we want to be careful not to over emphasize these questions. It remains possible that other questions might also tap into a specialized expertise, but, at least amount the 140 questions we tested, it appears that no topic appears frequently enough and that the questions are evenly distribution enough that no such additional expertise specialization emerges in any such obvious way.

It is also worth noting that there are questions with economic content that did not have large factor loadings on the economic factors. As such, our primary decision as a result of Pilot Study 1B was to omit the questions that loaded onto the economic factor for either accuracy or familiarity from further consideration.

The economic questions that did eventually wind up in the primary study were not questions that seemed to correlate quite so highly with this particular expertise specialty.

A.2. Primary Study Planning Pilot

Pilot Study 2 was conducted to aid in planning the design, anticipated attrition rates, and testing of materials ahead of the primary study. The goal of the primary study was to have approximately 1,000 participants complete all tasks across all seven waves. To accomplish this, we needed to decide on how many people we needed to recruit at the outset to account for and minimize attrition rates during the primary study. Thus, the purpose of Pilot Study 2 was to test study design options and incentive schemes to determine which, if any, would minimize attrition, and provide an estimate of how much attrition we might expect during the primary study. To accomplish this, Pilot Study 2 consisted of three waves: one forecasting wave and two waves of cognitive tasks, each matching content that was also included in the primary study.

A.2.1. Methods. Participants. Participants were recruited between September 1, 2023 and September 15, 2023. We recruited N = 1,199 participants via social media. Their mean age was 45.06, SD = 13.62, 783 (71.3%) were female, 279 (25.4%) male, 34 (3.1%) gender variant / non conforming, 1 something else, and 1 preferred not to say. 18 Design. The study followed a 3 (incentive condition) x 2 (recruitment condition) design. The three incentive conditions were: U-shaped, escalating, and backloaded. In the U-shaped condition, participants were paid $12.50 for completing the first wave, $5 for completing the second, and $12.50 for completing the third. In the escalating condition, participants were paid $5 for completing the first wave, $10 for completing the second, and $15 for completing the third. And in the backloaded condition, participants were paid $5 for completing each of the first two waves, and $20 for completing the third. In all three conditions, participants received guaranteed payment of $30 (the sum of each individual wave) for completing the full study. Figure A2 Scree Plot for the First 25 Components of the Parallel Analysis for sMAE Scores from Pilot 1B Figure A3 Scree Plot for the First 25 Components of the Parallel Analysis for Familiarity Ratings from Pilot 1B The recruitment condition either featured an initial unpaid introductory wave ("Wave 0") or did not. Participants who began with Wave 0 were recruited between September 1 st and 7 th of 2023, and completed two forecasting questions in each of the QEF and PEF. If they completed Wave 0, they were invited to complete Wave 1 the following week. Participants not in the Wave 0 condition were recruited between Procedure. For all participants, Wave 1 was made up of 15 forecasting questions in the QEF. Questions were drawn from the same item bank as the main study. See Supplementary list of items for items that were included in Pilot Study 2. All items had a resolution date at the end of September, 2023. The 10 participants who made the most accurate forecasts on average were each awarded a $25 bonus. Waves 2 and 3 were identical to waves 3 and 5 of the primary study. The 10 participants with the best mean Z -score standardized scores across cognitive tasks within each wave were awarded $25 bonuses.

A.2.2. Results. Across all conditions, N = 156 completed all three waves. Figure A4 shows the number of total completions by wave and experimental condition. Figure A5 shows the proportion of completions out of the number of people who started the study by wave and experimental condition. Figure A6 shows the proportion of total completions out of the number of people who completed Wave 1 by experimental condition. Figure A7 shows the attrition rate by wave, beginning with Wave 1.

A.2.3. Discussion.

Two key results emerged from Pilot Study 2. First, attrition was largest between participants' first and second wave and leveled off quickly after that. This included participants who participated in Wave 0. By Wave 3, the attrition levels were quite low in the Wave 0 condition, and considerably lower than the condition that did not feature Wave 0.

The results also suggested that the escalating payment condition suffered from lower attrition than the other incentive conditions, particularly compared to the U-shaped condition and in the condition that featured Wave 0. The escalating payment structure also provides an advantage over the U-shaped condition in terms of expected study cost, as the participants who do attrit out won't ever reach the higher payment waves.

Implications for Primary Study.

In planning the primary study, this led us to attempt to work backwards and decide how many total participants we would need to recruit to wind up with at least 1,000 people completing all seven waves. Based on the results from Pilot Study 2, in escalating payment and Wave 0 condition, attrition was just below 30% between Wave 0 and 1, below 20% between Wave 1 and 2, and below 5% between wave 2 and 3. Because Wave 0 was uncompensated, we worked backwards assuming 5% attrition for all waves after Wave 2, and 20% between waves 1 and 2, and determined that to end with at least 1,000 completers, we needed to target approximately N = 1,660 valid completions from Wave 1 that we would also invite to Wave 2. After each choice, there is a certain probability (volatility rate) that whichever option was worth fewer points will increase by 20, "leapfrogging" the previously higher-valued option. The goal is to select the option worth more points as frequently as possible by deciding how often to sample the unknown option (exploration) versus remain with the known option (exploitation).

LF has both an anchor version and an AIG version. The anchor version consists of 200 trials in which

the option values are fixed for all participants based on a previously chosen random set of outcomes with a volatility rate of 12.5%. The AIG version is randomly generated for each participant independently with an equivalent volatility rate and number of trials.

In the computational cognitive psychology literature, LF is typically used to compare individual participants' choice patterns to different model-based decision algorithms, to determine which models best approximate human behavior. It may be possible to use these model-based approaches to generate scoring rules; however, for simplicity, we scored participants based on the proportion of trials in which they selected the higher option. The intuition behind the inclusion of LF is that knowing how and when to explore new sources of information rather than exploit familiar ones is a skill that could plausibly benefit forecasting proficiency.

Impossible Question Criterion (IQC).

The IQC (Bennett and Steyvers 2022; see also Bereby-Meyer et al. 2003) is made up of a series of general knowledge questions with two possible answers. For most questions, only one of the two answers is factually correct. For the remaining questions, there is no factually correct answer (impossible questions). For each question, participants can choose to opt out or answer the question. If they do answer the question, a confidence rating is also elicited. The test provides scores for the number of correct answers to the general knowledge questions (GK), judgmental calibration for the confidence judgments (C), and the number of times they chose to opt out of impossible questions (IQ).

The original IQC item bank consists of 100 questions, including six impossible questions. We generated a shortened anchor version of the IQC using 24 of the questions with correct answers, as well as the six impossible questions. We then created two additional AIG versions by splitting 48 of the remaining questions from the original item bank in half and supplementing each half with six newly generated impossible questions. Impossible questions were generated by ChatGPT. See Appendix D for a list of the newly generated questions and the prompt used to generate them.

The intuition behind the inclusion of the IQC is that knowing the extent of one's knowledge and having well-calibrated confidence are skills that could plausibly benefit forecasting proficiency.

Denominator Neglect (DN). DN was inspired by a common decision bias of the same name. Participants make a series of choices between two proportions with the goal of selecting the larger proportion.

Research indicates that people will tend to erroneously favor proportions that have larger numerators, even when they represent smaller proportions (Stanovich and West 2008). Inclusion of visual arrays can reduce denominator neglect (Garcia-Retamero et al. 2010).

Each DN item features a choice between two boxes with a mix of gold and silver coins. The goal is to select the box with a larger proportion of gold coins. One box always contains 10 total coins (the small denominator option) with either one, two, or three gold coins. The other box always has 400 total coins (the large denominator option), with proportions ranging from plus (harmony trials) or minus (conflict trials) 1% to 8% the small denominator option in intervals of 1%.

There are two different designs of DN: separate (S) and combined (C).

In the separate design, options have only a verbal description or a visual array, but not both. Items can either be heterogeneous (one option verbal and the other visual) or homogeneous (both options verbal or both options visual). In the combined design, each option is represented by both a verbal description and a visual array. Both designs have an anchor and an AIG version. The anchor version of the separate design consists of a single set of randomly generated items. The AIG version randomizes whether and how each item will be homogeneous or heterogeneous independently for each participant. The anchor version of the combined design consists of a fixed set of randomly generated small denominator option proportions (10%, 20%, and 30%), and the AIG version randomly generates these proportions independently for each participant. Each design of DN has 48 items. DN is scored as the total number of cases in which the larger proportion is selected.

Success on DN is driven by how well one understands the importance of total population sizes, or base rates, when judging event outcomes. The intuition behind the inclusion of DN is that being aware of the importance of base rates and their implications for making probabilistic decisions is a skill that could plausibly benefit forecasting proficiency.

Bayesian Updating (BU).

BU is based on experiments by Phillips and Edwards (1966) in which participants must iteratively update their probabilistic judgments based on new information. Two boxes are displayed: one containing p red balls and 100 -p blue balls, the other containing p blue balls and 100 -p red balls, with p randomly set to either 60 or 70. At the start of each trial, one of the boxes is chosen at random with equal probability, but it is not revealed to participants which box it is. Five balls are then drawn from the chosen box, one at a time, with replacement. After the fifth draw, the task resets, and a new trial begins.

The test has two designs, easy and hard, each of which consists of eight trials with five sequential decisions.

In the easy design, after each ball is drawn, participants report the probability that the chosen box is the majority blue box. In the hard design, participants report the probability that the next draw will be a blue ball. Each design also has an AIG and an anchor version. In the anchor version, the sequence of draws is fixed for all participants, while in the AIG version, the draws are randomly generated for each participant independently.

BU scores are based on the absolute deviation between the estimate made in each trial and the optimal Bayesian estimate (see Appendix G for scoring details). The intuition behind the inclusion of BU is that following normative rules about how and how much to update one's probabilistic beliefs is a skill that could plausibly benefit forecasting proficiency.

Adult Decision-Making Competence: Resistance to Framing (RF). The Adult Decision-Making

Competence (ADMC) inventory is a battery of tests designed to assess decision-making ability (Bruine de Bruin et al. 2007). Though the ADMC is well validated, to our knowledge it has not previously been included in any forecasting studies.

RF is one of three subscales we considered for the FPT. The RF subscale consists of a series of comparisons between two options. Each comparison is repeated at two different points during the ADMC: once in a positive frame and again in a negative frame. For each comparison, participants rate their preference for the options on a scale of 1 to 6, with 1 representing extreme preference for the first option and 6 extreme preference for the second option.

Scores are based on consistency in judgment across the positively and negatively framed versions of each comparison. The ADMC-RF was adapted exactly as described in Bruine de Bruin et al. (2007), with the positively and negatively framed versions of each comparison split between the two cognitive test blocks.

The intuition behind the inclusion of ADMC-RF is that resisting the effects of irrelevant information, such as how information is framed, is a skill that could plausibly benefit forecasting proficiency.

Adult Decision-Making Competence: Risk Consistency (RC).

The RC subscale of the ADMC is similar to one of the CFS testlets: it assesses the consistency of risk assessments across timeframes.

Participants are asked to assess the probability that several events occur within a series of increasing time horizons. For each event, they first rate the probability that it will occur within one year. Later in the test, the same events are repeated, except participants must report the probability that they will occur within three years. The same events are later repeated once more with a time horizon of five years. Judgments are considered consistent when the probabilities monotonically increase for longer time horizons.

The ADMC-RC was adapted exactly as described in Bruine de Bruin et al. (2007). The intuition behind the inclusion of ADMC-RC is that following the normative rules of probability judgment is a skill that is known to benefit forecasting accuracy, and this test operationalizes that in a slightly different way than the CFS.

Adult Decision-Making Competence: Decision Rules (DR).

In the DR subscale of the ADMC, participants must assess how consumers should make purchasing decisions based on a set of stated preferences.

Each consumer specifies how they prioritize a set of feature ratings for a product they wish to purchase.

Participants must then decide which of several options best satisfies the consumer's preferences.

The ADMC-DR was adapted exactly as described in Bruine de Bruin et al. (2007), with one small modification: the product targets were televisions rather than DVD players. The intuition behind the inclusion of the ADMC-DR is that being able to optimize judgments based on an set of explicitly stated rules is a skill that could plausibly benefit forecasting proficiency.

Graph Literacy Scale (GL).

GL is designed to assess how well subjects make inferences from visual representations of data (Galesic and Garcia-Retamero 2011). It was originally developed in the context of medical decision-making and to our knowledge has not been previously validated in the context of a forecasting study. The test was adapted exactly as described in Galesic and Garcia-Retamero (2011). The intuition behind the inclusion of GL is that being able to make inferences based on data presented in a graphical format is a skill that could plausibly benefit forecasting proficiency.

Shipley-2.

The primary study featured one additional cognitive test: Shipley-2 (Shipley et al. 2009).

Shipley-2 is a proprietary test that must be licensed from the publisher for use. As such, it is not a candidate for inclusion in the FPT. However, it is a well-validated brief test of general intelligence. It consists of two subtests: Abstraction (A), which is an assessment of fluid intelligence, and Vocabulary (V ), which is an

Results indicated that subjects who most frequently opted out of impossible questions also showed the best accuracy in their probability judgments for questions with answers. The general knowledge questionnaire also provides a brief measure of crystallized intelligence, and the confidence ratings also provide a measure of calibration, consistent with the "classical method" of identifying forecasting ability (Colson and Cooke 2018), so this task has three outcome measures.

The original item bank from Bennett and Steyvers (2022) contains 100 total questions, six of which have no factually correct answers. The anchor form will include 24 of the 94 questions with correct answers, as well as all six impossible questions. The AIG procedure will be tested by splitting the remaining 48 of the remaining 70 questions into two separate forms of 24 (Form A and Form B). Form A and Form B will each be supplemented with six newly generated impossible questions, generated by feeding the original six impossible questions into ChatGPT. 19 There will be three primary scoring measures from the Impossible Question task: 1.

Proportion of impossible questions opted out of (Impossible Question-Impossible scores, IQI) Denominator Neglect. Denominator neglect is a known decision bias in which people rate proportions that are smaller as being superior if they have larger absolute values in the numerator (Stanovich and West 2008). For example, a 9 in 100 chance to win a lottery will be rated as superior to a chance of 1 in 10.

Additional research has shown that visual arrays in addition to verbal representations reduce denominator neglect (Garcia-Retamero et al. 2010).

Our version of the task is framed as a choice between two boxes with a mixture of gold and silver coins.

Selecting a gold coin is considered a success, and a silver coin a failure.

There are two versions of the task: one in which each option is either represented by only a verbal description or a visual representation (with each option randomized in each trial), and one where each option is represented by both a verbal description and visual representation. In each case, the small denominator lottery is based on a denominator of 10, with the proportion of successes being 10%, 20%, or 30%. The large denominator lottery is based on a denominator of 400, with the proportions ranging from plus or minus 1% to 8% of the small lottery (in intervals of 1%), for a total of 48 trials per version. The primary Denominator Neglect Score (DN) is the total number of cases in which the larger proportion is selected.

We may also consider harmony (the larger denominator option is also the larger proportion) vs conflict (the 19 See Appendix D or https://chat.openai.com/share/40bed4f5-0698-4d51-b003-e2c1f76b39ff for the prompt and questions generated.

larger denominator option is the smaller option) trial types, as well as comparisons involving differences in available information (verbal and visual) in exploratory analyses.

A.1. Question Selection Pilot Studies

The first two Pilot studies (Pilot 1A and 1B) were concerned with identifying a suitable list of forecasting questions to use in the primary study. We began with a database of 6,707 forecasting questions that were used in previous forecasting studies known as the autocast dataset (Zou et al. 2022). To reduce these to a more manageable starting point, we first manually filtered the items along several criteria:

Appendix C: Cognitive Test Details

For tests with extensive support in the forecasting literature and psychometric validation, we include only brief summaries and direct interested readers to the references. For the tests with less support in prior forecasting research or newly developed tests, we provide considerably more details.

The Cognitive Reflection Test (CRT).

The CRT is a measure of numerical reasoning ability in the face of an intuitively appealing distractor (Frederick 2005 , Atanasov and Himmelstein 2023 , Himmelstein et al. 2021 , Ho et al. 2024 , Mellers et al. 2015a). We used a 7-item version of the CRT (Toplak et al. 2014).

The Berlin Numeracy Scale (BN). BN is a 4-item measure of general numerical reasoning ability (Cokely et al. 2012 , Atanasov and Himmelstein 2023 , Himmelstein et al. 2021 , Ho et al. 2024 , Mellers et al. 2015a).

Matrix Reasoning (MR).

MR is a visual pattern matching test, variants of which are used in many standardized general intelligence tests (Raven 2000 , Atanasov and Himmelstein 2023 , Himmelstein et al. 2021 , Ho et al. 2024 , Mellers et al. 2015a). The version of matrix reasoning we used has an established AIG version, from which we drew 42 procedurally generated items which were fixed for all participants (Matzen et al. 2010).

Number Series (NS).

NS is a 9-item numerical pattern matching test (Dieckmann et al. 2017 , Atanasov and Himmelstein 2023 , Himmelstein et al. 2021).

The Coherence Forecasting Scale (CFS).

The CFS is a measure of how well people adhere to the logic of probability in their judgments. It is made up of 11 testlets which each involve 3-5 separate components.

CFS has an established AIG version made up of parallel item sets, from which we selected a single set which was fixed for all participants (Ho et al. 2024).

Time Series (TS).

TS is modified from experimental designs that require participants to extrapolate from time series graphs using a visual point-and-click interface (De Baets and Vanderheyden 2021, Reimers and Harvey 2011). For each item, participants see historical data from an unnamed time series that was generated by an underlying function with added Gaussian noise. They are required to predict the subsequent six points in the trend. The test is a 2 (noise level: high or low) x 2 (direction: ascending or descending) x 2 (type: linear or exponential) x 2 (number of historical datapoints: 10 or 30) design. Scores are computed as the mean squared deviation from the generative function.

There were two different versions of TS: an AIG version, in which the historical data was generated independently for each trial, and an anchor version, in which the historical data was fixed for each combination of noise, direction, type, and number of historical datapoints.

Though similar tasks have been used in forecasting research, the context has typically been to study population-level behaviors, rather than measure forecasting proficiency. The intuition behind the inclusion of TS is that using visual information to extrapolate trends is a plausible skill that could benefit forecasters' accuracy.

Leapfrog (LF). LF is a tractable bandit-style task designed to measure optimal exploration vs. exploitation tendencies (Knox et al. 2012). It consists of a set of binary choices between two options. To start, one option is worth 0 points and the other is worth 10 points. Each time a choice is selected, its point value is

Appendix G: Scoring Rules for Cognitive Tasks

What follows is information about the specific scoring rules for the time series, leapfrog, impossible question, denominator neglect, and Bayesian updating tasks. All other scoring rules can be found in references associated with each task.

Time Series. This task is based on work by De Baets and Vanderheyden (2021) and Reimers and Harvey (2011) in which people are asked to extrapolate from graphical time series using a visual point-and-click interface. On each trial, participants will see historical data from an unnamed time series, generated by an underlying function with added noise, and be required to predict the subsequent five points in the trend. The task is a 2 (noise level: high vs low) x 2 (direction: ascending or descending) x 2 (type: linear or exponential) x 2 (historical data: 10 points or 30 points) design, with one item for each combination per form, and two forms (a 16 item anchor form and a 16 item AIG form).

Primary Time Series Scores (TS) are computed as the Mean Squared Deviation from the generative function. Other potential scoring options include proneness to known biases such as trend damping and adding noise, which may be included in exploratory analyses. Exploratory analyses will also compare the effectiveness of scores from different conditions in terms of how well they predict accuracy.

Leapfrog. The leapfrog task is a tractable bandit-style task designed to measure optimal explore vs exploit tendencies (Knox et al. 2012). The task is a set of binary choices between two options. To start, one option is worth 0 points and the other is worth 10 points. Each time a choice is selected, its point value is revealed, but the alternative not chosen remains hidden. After each choice, there is a certain probability (volatility rate) whichever option was worth fewer points will "leapfrog" the option worth more points and increase by 20. So if option A is originally 10 and option B 0, at some point option B will become 20 while A remains 10. Then A will eventually become 30 while B stays at 20. The goal is to select the option worth more points as frequently as possible. The Anchor form will consist of 200 trials in which the option values are pre-determined based on a random set of outcomes with a volatility rate of 12.5%. The AIG form will be a randomly generated series with an equivalent volatility rate and number of trials. Primary Leapfrog Scores (LF) are based on the proportion of trials in which participants selected the higher option. There are also several model based assessments of optimal decision making which can be explored (see Knox et al. 2012).

Impossible Question Criterion.

The impossible question criterion is a task developed by Bennett and Steyvers (2022) (see also Bereby-Meyer et al. 2003). In this task, subjects are given a series of general knowledge problems with two possible answers. For the majority of questions, one of the two options is factually correct, and the other is not. For a minority of questions, there is no factually correct answer. For each question, participants can choose to opt out or answer the question. Participants also provide confidence ratings when they do not opt out.

For example, a question with a factually correct answer is Greenhouse effect refers to: a. Gasses in the atmosphere that trap heat (correct) b. Impact to the earth's ozone layer A question without a factually correct answer is Scoring Rule: )︃⃓ ⃓ ⃓ ⃓ = Absolute Error of log odds on trial j Person level scores will then be computed as Bayesian Update Source Score (BAS) = mean(le j,easy ) and Bayesian Update Forecast Score (BAF) = mean(le j,hard ) for each person.

Standardization One shortcoming of sample standardization is that it requires a large number of forecasters to estimate the sample statistics Āk and S A k . For questions with historical time series, such as those used in this study, an alternative is to standardize prior to scoring for accuracy based on historical information. For each such forecasting question, where available (see supplementary materials), we recorded historical trends at monthly intervals from December 2022 through April 2024.

Overconfidence/calibration on possible questions, calculated as mean(Confidence) -IQG (Impossible Question-Overconfidence scores, IQO) in which people must iteratively update their probabilistic judgments based on new information.

In this task, two boxes are displayed, one containing p red balls and 100 -p blue balls. The other contains p blue balls and 100 -p red balls (in our version, p is either 60 or 70). One of the boxes is chosen at random with equal probability. Five balls are drawn one at a time with replacement. The task has two versions. In the Source version, after each drawn ball, subjects must report the probability that the box is the majority red or majority blue box. In the Forecast version, subjects must report the probability the next draw will be a blue ball. In the anchor j = Number of successes = Number of blue balls drawn through draw j f j = Number of failures = Number of red balls drawn through draw j L j = Likelihood Ratio given data after draw j = (︃ P (Blue) blue urn P (Blue) red urn )︃ s j -f j Ω 1j = LΩ0 = Posterior Odds of blue urn after draw j For source (easy) version: pj,easy = subjects' reported probability of reference (blue) urn after draw jError of log odds on trial j For forecast (hard) version pj,hard = subjects' reported probability of blue ball after draw j u j = Ω 1j 1 + Ω 1j true probability of blue urn after draw j p j,hard = u j P (Blue) + (1 -u j ) (1 -P (Blue)) = true probability of blue ball on next draw

Appendix H: Data and Code Availability All data, code used to process the raw data, and code used to program cognitive tests 22 are publicly at https://github.com/forecastingresearch/fpt. All Qualtrics survey files containing forecasting questions and data analysis code can be found in the supplementary materials at https://osf.io/q2e94/? view_only= 73cacdfbc12b4e60adbc220e5341d661. All data analyses were conducted in R version 4.3.0 (R Core Team 2023) using the following packages: tidyverse (Wickham et al. 2019), lme4 (Bates et al. 2015), lavaan (Rosseel 2012), pROC (Robin et al. 2011), emmeans (Lenth 2023), domir (Luchman 2024), and chemometrics (Filzmoser 2023).

The terms fixed-variable format and probability elicitation format are interchangeable, as are the terms fixedprobability format and quantile elicitation format. In each case, the former term refers to the features of the probability distribution held constant by the elicitation, while the latter term refers to the features of the probability distribution the forecaster is required to report. To avoid confusion, we will use the terms probability elicitation format (PEF) and quantile elicitation format (QEF) throughout.

The primary study was preregistered on the Open Science Foundation. Preregistration and supplementary materials can be found at https://osf.io/q2e94/? view_only=73cacdfbc12b4e60adbc220e5341d661

For both Brier and S-scores, less than 1% of forecasts produces standardized scores with magnitudes greater than five. However, the largest of these for Brier scores was 7.30, while the largest for S-scores was 58.16, so Winsorization was designed to address unwanted leverage of a small number of observations, some of which likely reflected input errors rather than poor judgment(Zhu et al. 2026), rather than quantity of outliers.

The logic for this is the same as for Winsorizing sample standardized scores, in that it is more a concern about leverage of extreme outliers than the quantity of outliers, though in this case, 9.1% of forecasts were Winsorized.

Note that we use scaled rather than standardized accuracy so that question effects can vary as a function of time.

We used DN-C and BU-H (excluding DN-S and BU-E) to reduce redundancy and excluded the Shipley-2 subscales since they are proprietary and cannot be used in the final FPT.

Given our large sample size, we focus on effect size rather than statistical significance, as even extremely small effects proved statistically significant.

MR and CFS have previously validated AIG versions(Matzen et al. 2010 , Ho et al. 2024).

Scores were reversed to conform to traditional testing conventions where higher, rather than lower scores reflect better performance.

Note that some of these definitions only work under our specific setup where certain conditions are met, e.g. the urns have exactly inverse probabilities.

Conservatism, as 0 < c < 1 is the modal empirical finding.
